Exploration yields weapons like a handgun and rocket launcher, ammunition, rations and gadgets like a gas mask. Hostages held in the base can be rescued. The Famicom version reworks several aspects of the MSX2 original, changes that led Kojima to disown it. It's the same game as the NES Metal Gear.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — Stealth and exploration are visual, but item and radio text is Japanese and helps with progress.
nes_counterpart_context: Released in North America as Metal Gear (1988).

gameplay_summary: Licensed action-adventure: as Superman (and Clark Kent), travel Metropolis via an overhead map to side-scrolling locations, fight Lex Luthor and Kryptonian criminals, and use super powers that run on energy.
dossier: Kemco's Superman, released first in Japan. An overhead map of Metropolis leads to side-scrolling areas, with animated scenes along the way. Superman has stamina plus 'super power' energy bars, and collected icons power a limited supply of abilities: X-ray vision, flight, super spin, heat vision and super breath. The story pits him against Lex Luthor and a gang of criminals exiled from Krypton. The Japanese release plays a synthesised version of John Williams's film theme, which the US version replaced with music from Kemco's Indora no Hikari.
language_barrier_reason: MEDIUM — The action is visual, but in-game text is presumably Japanese on Famicom; the extent is not confirmed in the sources.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Superman, published in North America by Seika (1988) rather than Kemco.
japanese_version_notes: Uses a synthesised arrangement of the 1978 film's Superman theme; the NES version replaced it with music from Indora no Hikari.

gameplay_summary: First-person dungeon RPG: create a party of up to six from five races, three alignments and four basic classes, then map ten floors of the Mad Overlord's maze to defeat the wizard Werdna.
dossier: ASCII's arranged Famicom version of the 1981 classic, developed by Game Studio. The town is a set of menus where you roll characters (Human, Elf, Dwarf, Gnome, Hobbit; good, neutral or evil; Fighter, Mage, Priest, Thief) and, with luck and levels, reach the elite Bishop, Samurai, Lord and Ninja classes. The maze is ten floors of first-person corridors; on most floors the goal is to find the stairs or elevator down alive, and at the bottom waits Werdna, who stole Trebor's amulet. Good and evil characters normally can't share a party. On Famicom, floors 6 to 8 are redesigned, and ASCII's Turbo File can store a backup.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — Menu-driven RPG with Japanese menus, spells and messages; the spells especially need reading or a reference sheet.
nes_counterpart_context: Same game as the NES Wizardry: Proving Grounds of the Mad Overlord, published in North America by Nexoft (1990) rather than ASCII.
japanese_version_notes: Floors 6 to 8 are redesigned compared with the original computer version, and the cartridge supports ASCII's Turbo File for save backups.

gameplay_summary: Licensed RPG: as Kitaro, travel through six regions of Japan sealed by demon-cloud barriers, reach each region's boss via underground caves, and defeat the nine-tailed fox's yokai army to rescue Yumeko.
dossier: Bandai's second GeGeGe no Kitaro game, now an RPG. Japan is split into six areas (Kanto, Tohoku, Chubu-Kinki, Chugoku-Shikoku, Kyushu and a mysterious continent). Every area except your Kanto starting point is sealed by demon-cloud barriers, so you have to find the underground caves that connect them. Each area has a boss, and some can only be reached with key items, which adds adventure elements. Unusually, there's no money: items are found or given by jizo statues. Battles feature animation, which was praised at the time, but criticised points include tough ordinary enemies that give only 1 experience point, slow pacing, and a 'search' command that never does anything.
language_barrier_reason: HIGH — A text-driven RPG with Japanese dialogue and menus; finding key items depends on it.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Updated Famista baseball: the same quick arcade-style game with player stats, retuned toward pitching with a smaller batter's box movement range and refreshed rosters.
dossier: A minor update to Namco's hit Pro Baseball Family Stadium. It was sold in nearly the same box with an '87 sticker, which is why some references call it the '87-season edition. The main change in play is balance: batters have less room to move in the box, so it favours pitchers more than the original. On-screen stat labels switch from AV/HR/ER to Japanese characters. There's still just the one stadium, Pikkari Stadium. Fans of the first game will find it familiar, with updated teams.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Baseball is universal; player names and stat labels are Japanese but not needed to play.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan. The original Pro Baseball Family Stadium is a separate census identity with its own western counterpart; this update stayed in Japan.

gameplay_summary: Space Harrier-style 3D shooter: fly schoolgirl Nokko into the screen, dodging obstacles and shooting animal monsters with a submachine gun across six stages, with optional Famicom 3D goggles.
dossier: A Pony Canyon pseudo-3D shooter that copies Space Harrier almost exactly, with a delinquent schoolgirl heroine. Nokko's best friend has been kidnapped by the Animal School alliance, and she sets off with a submachine gun through areas full of vicious koalas, monster lizards, baboons, sea serpents and giant spiders, toward the two-headed serpent Orochi. She flies freely around the screen, avoiding indestructible obstacles and shooting enemies, and one hit costs a life. Her outfit changes by stage, from sailor uniform to gym clothes to school swimsuit. It's harder than its model, with fast enemies. It supports the Famicom 3D System goggles. Reviews were poor.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Shooting action; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Supports the Famicom 3D System active-shutter goggles.

gameplay_summary: Floor-mat game show: run, jump and stomp on the Family Trainer mat through obstacle challenges from the TV show Takeshi's Castle, finishing with a cart battle against Takeshi.
dossier: A Family Trainer game based on Beat Takeshi's cult TV show, in which ordinary contestants storm a castle through absurd physical challenges. You play the challenges on the mat, using your feet to run, jump and avoid hazards through a series of difficult stages. The goal is to beat the castle's lord, Takeshi himself. The finale has you steering a cart with the mat. It's exhausting and luck-dependent: on GameCenter CX, Arino needed five hours and a lot of stamina to finish it.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Physical mat play; nothing needs reading.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
japanese_version_notes: Requires the Family Trainer mat (Famicom expansion port).

gameplay_summary: Top-down F1 racing: tune your car's setup, save it by password, and race fast-scrolling circuits where rival cars can't collide with you but walls and barriers can wreck you.
dossier: Namco's racing game designed by Masanobu Endo (Xevious, Druaga) at Game Studio, and a Famitsu Gold Hall of Fame game (32/40). It's a one-player, top-down Formula racer focused on car setup: you adjust the machine freely and save your settings with a password. Unusually, there's no collision between cars, so you pass straight through rivals, but hitting trackside obstacles at speed is an instant crash and retirement. The fast, smooth scrolling and the pit crew animation were praised. The start/finish tower is modelled on Suzuka's, reflecting Namco's sponsorship there. the name became a series.
language_barrier_reason: LOW — Racing with mostly visual setup screens; the password is the only text to manage.
nes_counterpart_context: No NES counterpart; released only in Japan.
